  • Every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan.
  • In a recent development, so what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan. Following the latest update from the CA/Browser Forum, the maximum lifetime of a certificate has fallen from 398 days to 200, and it will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Renewal is no longer an annual chore. It’s an ongoing task that only stays manageable with automation.

In a recent development, so what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes? For many setups, very little will change. For others, one missed renewal can mean an outage. This article explains what’s changing and what to do if you’re in the second group.

Today, an SSL certificate is valid for 200 days at most. The limit applies when a certificate is issued, so the ones you already hold keep their original expiration date.

Where you feel it depends on how your certificates renew. Sites on managed hosting platforms or behind a content delivery network (CDN) usually renew automatically already, often every 90 days, so the upcoming limit changes little. The pressure lands on setups where someone buys a certificate once a year and installs it by hand. At 47 days, that becomes about 12 renewals a year.

Industry observers note that A certificate is a promise from a certificate authority that a key really belongs to a domain, and that promise gets less reliable the longer it runs. If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, it stays usable until it expires. Cutting the lifetime shrinks that window, so a problem that once lingered for over a year is now fixed in weeks.

According to recent reports, shorter lifetimes also make revocation, the process for canceling a bad certificate, far less critical. Revocation has never worked perfectly, but a certificate that expires within weeks matters much less if a cancellation doesn’t reach every browser.

According to recent reports, another reason is about people. A task done once a year is easy to forget and hard to check from outside. Browser makers have pushed for years to move the industry onto automatic renewal, on the logic that a process that runs every few weeks gets tested constantly. If it breaks, you notice quickly instead of discovering it on the day the certificate expires.

According to recent reports, for most people, the first effect is simply more work. A certificate that once needed attention every year will soon need it every few weeks. Plus, each renewal is a small chance for something to go wrong. Multiply that by dozens of sites, mail servers, and devices, and the chance of one slipping through grows quickly.

The safety nets are also thinner. If you relied on the renewal emails, nothing is watching your certificates now. Additionally, with a shorter life, there’s less time between this should have renewed and this has expired.

It has been revealed that an expired certificate doesn’t make a site slow or dated. It makes it unreachable for most visitors. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all show a full-page warning that the connection isn’t private, and most people leave instead of clicking through. If the site uses HSTS, a setting that tells browsers to connect only over secure links, there is often no way to click through at all, and visitors are blocked outright until the certificate is fixed.

Industry observers note that the damage doesn’t stop at the home page. Checkouts, contact forms, and logins that depend on the secure connection fail along with it, often without an error message that points at the real cause. Other systems break, too, because apps and integrations that call your site over a secure link refuse to connect to an expired certificate.

Sources indicate that nothing about your site has to change for any of this to happen. A date passes, and a site that worked on Friday is down on Monday. In a 47-day lifetime, that date comes around about every six weeks.

Recent findings suggest that automatic renewal tools do the heavy lifting well. The failures happen around them:.

Look at the five failures above and you’ll see what they share. Each one happens quietly. The renewal job ran, or looked like it did, and nobody checked what the server was actually serving afterwards. Automation can tell you it tried. It can’t tell you the result reached your visitors.

What closes that gap is a check that never relies on your server’s own account of events. Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring does exactly that. It reads the certificate installed on your web server from the cloud, the way a visitor’s browser would, and alerts you before it expires, using thresholds you choose. If a renewal fails quietly, you hear about it from the monitor and not from a customer.

Recent findings suggest that for each certificate, it records the issuing authority, the owner, the issue date, the expiration date, and the days remaining, including on servers that host several certificates behind one address. That last number matters more as lifespans shrink. When a certificate lasts 47 days, the days left is the figure that tells you a renewal is overdue, and you can set your warning against it using the quarter-of-the-lifetime rule covered next.

Once a monitor is watching your certificates, the next question is when it should speak up.

Industry observers note that most expiration alerts are set to a fixed number of days: warn at 30 days left and escalate at seven. That works for a certificate that lasts a year and renews with a month to spare. It breaks when the whole certificate lasts for a limited number of days.

Recent findings suggest that here’s why: a healthy certificate renews with about a third of its life still left. If your alert appears earlier than that, it goes off on certificates that are doing nothing wrong, and soon everyone ignores it. As lifespans shrink, a fixed 30-day alert will start doing exactly that.

According to recent reports, the fix is to set the alerts based on lateness, not on how close the expiry date is. Warn when a quarter of the lifetime is left, since a renewal is overdue by then, and escalate when a tenth is left. Because these are shares of the lifetime, they keep working, however short lifespans get.

The next cut lands on March 15, 2027, so a few checks now will save you from scrambling later:.

Shorter lifespans won’t break your site, but a missed renewal will, so fix the quiet failures now while a mistake still costs an afternoon to fix, not a Monday morning outage affecting lots of customers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A top House Democrat is broadening his investigation into Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital fund 1789 Capital by demanding records from four companies that secured an investment before benefiting from lucrative federal contracts or policies.Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee and the panel’s incoming chair, sent letters on Monday evening to the defense contractor Hadrian Automation, vape maker Juul Labs, prediction market platform Polymarket and the online firearms seller GrabAGun.The Maryland congressman requested that each firm send him two years’ worth of communications with 1789 Capital and other select documents, saying the materials would help him investigate whether U.S. President Donald Trump’s eldest son used insider information to orchestrate or anticipate government actions that boosted the companies and his own finances. The investigation was opened over the summer Both Trump Jr. and 1789 Capital, which is based in Palm Beach, Florida, deny any wrongdoing.The letters ramp up an investigation that Raskin opened in August into Trump Jr.’s firm, which he said “suddenly struck investment gold” after naming the president’s son as a partner in 2024. As one of the lawmakers who will be spearheading Democrats’ oversight of the Trump administration when they take control of Congress in January, Raskin has said that uncovering information about bribery and financial corruption will be among his top priorities.Trump Jr. has repeatedly rejected accusations that he has exploited government access for profit. At an Axios event last week, he acknowledged that he understood people’s corruption concerns, but said that they weren’t accurate, noting he has been an investor for decades.“I can see what they are saying. It doesn’t make it so,” he said. “The notion that I should somehow sit in a corner, suck my thumb and wait, you know, eight years — in this case 12 years — till we’re out of the political game, it’s not real.” Trump Jr. and the firm deny any wrongdoing 1789 Capital also has forcefully denied claims of wrongdoing. In a letter to Raskin in September, the company’s lawyers defended the firm’s investment thesis as predating Trump’s administration and said that while it “welcomes legitimate congressional oversight,” it “has no intention of being held hostage to political gamesmanship.”On Monday, the company’s attorney, Bill Burck, said the September letter explained flaws in Raskin’s understanding, but Raskin “never bothered to reply.”“Facts are facts and Congressman Raskin has them wrong here, but persists in his tall tales against 1789,” Burck said. “These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence.” ‘Serendipitous timing’ of investments, Raskin states in letters The firm was founded in 2022 and Trump Jr. was announced as a partner in November 2024.In his letters to the four companies obtained by The Associated Press, Raskin outlined how federal policies or contracts had benefited their businesses and claimed that 1789 Capital had suspiciously “serendipitous timing” when it invested in them.Hadrian Automation, he wrote, received nearly $1 billion in U.S. Navy and Army contracts in March — its first-ever federal contracts — after bringing 1789 Capital on as an investor in 2025.Juul, Raskin wrote, received Food and Drug Administration clearance to keep its electronic cigarette products on the market in July 2025, four months after 1789 Capital had taken a stake in the company.The congressman wrote that GrabAGun got help from 1789 to go public and put Trump Jr. on its board before the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives issued a proposed rule to ease the process of shipping guns to people’s homes. Raskin calls Trump administration order ‘blatantly unlawful’ Raskin also raised questions about the Justice Department and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission closing investigations into Polymarket in July 2025, after 1789 Capital already had invested in the prediction market platform.GrabAGun said in a statement that Raskin’s letter “is a political document, and its allegations are baseless.”“ATF’s review of its regulations was well known across the firearms industry, and the agency published numerous proposed rules for public comment. GrabAGun’s only input came through public comments on several of those proposals,” the statement read.Juul Labs said that it was reviewing its letter closely.“As always, we intend to cooperate with any Congressional effort to understand our company, our commitment to combating underage vaping, and our mission to help adult smokers of combustible cigarettes transition completely away from smoking,” it said in an emailed response.The other recipients of the letters didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.The Trump administration has taken steps to push back on the Democrats’ oversight efforts, including an executive order on Friday directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged.That could complicate compliance with Raskin’s investigation for at least one of the companies, Hadrian Automation, which is a federal contractor.Raskin has called Trump’s order “blatantly unlawful” and said that public contractors have a “duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls.” —Ali Swenson, Associated Press.

After the better part of 7 years, Samsung’s mobile division has a fresh chief and it’s Choi Won-Joon, who is already off to a great start with the successful launch of Galaxy Z Fold 8.

According to recent reports, in an announcement today, Samsung confirmed some shuffling of its executive team, most notably with the end of TM Roh’s tenure as the head of Samsung’s MX business unit. In other words, there’s a newly introduced captain at the helm for Samsung’s mobile division, and it’s Choi Won-Joon.

Won-Joon has been the Chief Operating Officer of Samsung’s MX unit since March of 2025, and more recently oversaw the launch of Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold 8, appearing on stage at both launch events and in behind-the-scenes meetings with the press.

Choi Won-joon, Head of the MX Business Unit at Samsung Electronics’ DX Division, has held positions such as Head of the Next-Generation Product Development Team, Head of the Strategic Product Development Team, and Head of Development at the MX Business Unit. Since being appointed President and Chief Operating Officer (COO) of the MX Business Unit in March 2025, he has led the successive successes of the Galaxy S26 and Z Fold 8. Based on the know-how accumulated while leading the development of the Galaxy series for a long time, he is expected to lead innovation in foldable phones, on-device AI, and wearables.

It has been revealed that TM Roh isn’t leaving the organization, but will drop his responsibilities in the mobile division. He remains one of two CEOs at Samsung alongside Jeon Young-hyun.

#184444. Latest Update: The Missing Layer In Enterprise AI Is The Human

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (973 w)

Latest Update: The Missing Layer In Enterprise AI Is The Human

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vivek Bhaskaran is founder & CEO of QuestionPro, a global leader in survey and research, data and insights services.
  • In 2025, a request kept showing up in our customer conversations: “Please disable AI in your app.
  • Twelve months later, same customers, opposite request: “Turn AI on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vivek Bhaskaran is founder & CEO of QuestionPro, a global leader in survey and research, data and insights services.

In 2025, a request kept showing up in our customer conversations: “Please disable AI in your app. We’re not allowed to use it.”.

Twelve months later, same customers, opposite request: “Turn AI on. Teach us how to use it.”.

I have been running QuestionPro since 2005. I have never seen buyer sentiment flip that fast. The wait-and-see crowd went all in, almost overnight. The models got genuinely good at reasoning, and agents started doing the work instead of just chatting about it. The fog burned off.

But once the fog lifts, you can see what is actually missing. And what is missing in most enterprise AI is not more intelligence. It is people.

Consider the pace. In 2018, AI models could barely string together a coherent sentence. By 2022, they could write basic HTML. In 2026, they are working through math problems that sat unsolved for 90 years. It took humanity 66 years to go from the first powered flight to landing on the moon. We are compressing that kind of leap into a few product cycles.

It has been revealed that every firm now has access to roughly the same brilliant brain. You rent it. Your competitor rents it. That brain knows everything about the world, but almost nothing about your company.

Think of it as the smartest new hire you have ever made, permanently stuck on day one. Today, most enterprise AI works like this: You type a prompt, it gives a response. The AI only knows what you tell it, and the answer is only as good as your prompt.

Sources indicate that the next phase will likely be different. AI is expected to pull in organizational context on its own, including your customers, market, people, strategy, rulebooks and regulatory and compliance obligations. Context is what turns general intelligence into an answer that actually fits your business.

What Leaders Can Take From This: Stop measuring your AI strategy by which AI model you picked. Measure it by what your AI knows about your organization that a competitor’s AI does not.

Sources indicate that much of that context is documents, or policies, contracts, playbooks and compliance rules. Those are relatively easy to plug in. Point the agent at the folder and you are halfway there.

It has been revealed that the hard part is human context. Why customers actually churn. What employees say when they think leadership is not listening. How a market feels about your price increase before it shows up in the revenue line. None of that lives in a PDF. It lives with your voice-of-customer programs, your research teams and your employee experience teams.

It has been revealed that for years, insights teams have been treated as a reporting function. They are the people who send the 40-slide deck that gets skimmed five minutes before the board meeting. That era is over. In an AI-driven manufacturer, insights teams become infrastructure. They supply the human signal that every AI system and every AI-informed decision depends on.

This changed how I lead. I stopped asking my team, “What AI features should we ship?” and started asking, “What does our AI still not understand about humans?” The second question produces far better roadmaps.

What Leaders Can Take From This: Find out where your insights, CX and EX teams sit in your AI roadmap. If the answer is “They get the output later,” then you have your org chart upside down.

Here is a test I like. Take two customers who look identical in your data. Same age bracket, same ZIP code, same purchase history, same plan tier. On a spreadsheet, they are twins.

Recent findings suggest that now, ask them why they bought from you. You will often find they are worlds apart. One is a loyal fan. The other is one bad support ticket away from leaving.

That is the difference between being profiled and being understood. Behavioral data profiles people. Only asking people, and listening to the answer, produces understanding. AI is extraordinary at the first. Without a human-context layer, it is guessing at the second, very confidently.

Recent findings suggest that there is a data quality trap here, too. As AI gets better at generating responses, it also gets better at faking them. Bots and synthetic answers are flooding research the same way spam once flooded inboxes. You need to know which data came from a verified, real human being. Feed an AI fake people and it will make very precise decisions about customers who do not exist.

What Leaders Can Take From This: Ask your vendors and your own teams how they verify that human data is actually human. If nobody can answer swiftly, that is your answer.

Sources indicate that I ride motorcycles, and I have ridden in more than a dozen countries. Riding is a great equalizer. It puts you far from the boardroom and close to how most people actually live. Every trip reminds me that people are more surprising, more contradictory and more interesting than any dataset suggests.

One of our customers summed it up better than I can: Customers like talking to people.

Technology can accelerate our knowledge and expertise, but it will never replace authenticity and connection. The companies that prove most successful in the next decade will not be the ones that remove humans from the loop. They will be the ones whose AI understands humans best.

Recent findings suggest that that is the missing layer. It is human. And the good news is that you already have it. You just have to plug it in.

In a recent development, forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

#184443. Google broke its biggest promise about Gmail. It’s the 1 thing no company should ever do

📖 Baca

Google broke its biggest promise about Gmail. It’s the 1 thing no company should ever do

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Promises, by their very nature, are inconvenient.
  • Recent findings suggest that promises, by their very nature, are inconvenient.
  • Of course, the benefit of all that inconvenience is that people trust you when you keep your promises.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Promises, by their very nature, are inconvenient. You tell someone you’re going to do something, and then you have to do it. Or, you promise you’ll never do something, and now you’ve restricted your options. Of course, the benefit of all that inconvenience is that people trust you when you keep your promises. And trust, as I’ve written before, is your most valuable asset, especially when you’re a massive manufacturer whose entire business depends on the willingness of your customers to give you their personal information. Like Google. Which is why it was such a big deal back in 2017 when Google promised it would not scan your Gmail in order to show you personalized ads. Previously, Google would scan your email to decide which ads to show. People didn’t love that, so Google told customers their data was their own and wouldn’t be used for ads. For almost a decade, that was the deal. You could use Gmail, Google Photos, and Google Drive without worrying that the information you stored in those services would be used as a source of ad recommendations. Earlier this month, however, the company quietly updated its privacy policy to say that it would use information from Gmail, Google Photos, and Google Drive to influence the ads people see. Specifically, the policy—which took effect October 16—claims that information from those services can be used to personalize advertisements when customers choose to connect them to other Google products that have personalized advertising. The most obvious reason Google is doing this is Personal Intelligence, which lets users connect their Gmail, Search, and Photos to Gemini. The reason you might want to do this is that it turns out that AI can be very useful at pulling information from your email, for example. Of course, that’s very different from wanting Google to then show you ads based on what it finds. To be clear, it’s not that Google is suddenly scanning everyone’s inbox to sell ads. You have to turn on the connection—it’s off by default. In addition, Google isn’t giving your personal information to advertisers, and it says it doesn’t directly target ads based on the data you have in those services. Instead, Google’s AI can use information derived from connected apps to personalize ads. I’m sure there’s some kind of technical distinction there, but I don’t know that it’s all that meaningful if you’re someone who has trusted Google with all your information. Say, for example, you are planning a trip, and you ask Gemini to help you strategy activities when you’re there. You give it access to your email so it can find your flights and then track whether the price changes. That’s super useful, and it’s the kind of thing that AI tools are actually really good at. Imagine, however, if suddenly you started seeing ads for things to do near your travel destination. Under Google’s latest policy, information derived from that reservation could definitely influence the advertisements you see. Look, it’s not that Google is doing something inherently wrong. You can certainly decide for yourself whether you want to connect your accounts at all. Also, to its credit, Google is disclosing how that information might be used. The problem is that Google is changing the terms of a promise it made in order to earn people’s trust in the first place. And you can’t connect Personal Intelligence and take advantage of its genuine benefits without opting in to the ad part. Every company eventually faces a situation where keeping a promise it made to its users suddenly becomes inconvenient. Maybe it’s because the market changes, or because its competitors introduce something new, or there’s an opportunity to make more money. When that happens, it’s tempting to find a technical reason for changing the terms of the deal. Google could reasonably argue that its new policy is different from its old practice because users have to opt in and their emails aren’t directly used to select advertisements. But you don’t build trust with technical distinctions in your privacy policy. You build it by being clear about what customers can expect, and then doing exactly that. In Google’s case, the promise was simple: We won’t use the information you put in Gmail to personalize advertising. Now, if you want to connect your personal information to Google’s AI product, it will. The most important thing a company can do is keep its promises, especially when doing so becomes inconvenient. The worst thing that can happen is that customers start wondering which promises you’ll keep and which ones you’ll change when you see a better business opportunity. Once that happens, you’ve already lost something far more valuable than whatever you hoped to gain. —Jason Aten This article originally appeared on Fast Company’s sister website, Inc.com. Once that happens, you’ve already lost something far more valuable than whatever you hoped to gain.

—Jason Aten.

Breaking: Leaders: transformation should not be your focus

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1359 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in his 1980 book Managing in Turbulent Times, management guru Peter Drucker wrote, “The greatest danger in times of turbulence is not the turbulence; it is to act with yesterday’s logic.” This seems obvious.
  • According to recent reports, in his 1980 book Managing in Turbulent Times, management guru Peter Drucker wrote, “The greatest danger in times of turbulence is not the turbulence; it is to act with yesterday’s logic.” This seems obvious.
  • It may be tempting to think that the other side of turbulence is overhauling the organization in a major transformation effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in his 1980 book Managing in Turbulent Times, management guru Peter Drucker wrote, “The greatest danger in times of turbulence is not the turbulence; it is to act with yesterday’s logic.” This seems obvious. But more often than not, businesses lean into safe, tried and true, old-school thinking as their life raft during uncertain times. Consider Nvidia, initially defending keeping Jensen Huang in place as CEO amidst accusations of major ethical missteps. It may be tempting to think that the other side of turbulence is overhauling the organization in a major transformation effort. But Geoff Tuff and Steve Goldbach, who are leaders in Deloitte’s sustainability practice, have a different take on moving through organizational turbulence. They believe that large-scale transformation is not the right focus. In fact, their research and experience show that organizations who focus on transformation tend to fail. What they offer instead is an alternative view that is compellingly explored in their book Hone: How Purposeful Leaders Defy Drift. Cumulatively, Geoff and Steve have decades of experience working with Fortune 500 companies that end up drifting in the process of trying to transform. When I recently spoke with them they shared that “drift” is the unintentional, imperceptible shift that leaves an organization uncompetitive because leaders fail to make micro-adjustments along the way. The solution? Hone: make small, intentional continuous adjustments to stay on course rather than wait until a massive disruption is necessary. Here are my three biggest takeaways from our conversation. 1. Honing is the antidote to failed transformation. Broad-scale transformations carry a 70% failure rate because humans naturally resist drastic change. This leads to organizational “tissue rejection.” Instead replace massive transformation with continuous “honing” to prevent drift. Geoff’s pastime and love of sailing have clearly influenced their perspective. Because just like adjusting a boat’s autopilot to account for winds and currents, leaders should focus on honing (for example, micro-adjustments in leadership style, accountability, KPI’s, etc.)  to stay on course rather than wait until a massive, disruptive transformation is required. 2. AI can help identify where honing is needed. Invisible drift can be made visible because AI can detect subtle patterns and organizational drift that are otherwise invisible to the human eye, enabling managers to address complications proactively. An AI enabled organizational network analysis can track thousands of interactions over time (such as email and Slack messages about meetings). For example, it can spot if an engineering team’s contact with the product team has decreased over 30% over multiple quarters. A 2021 study published in Nature Human Behaviour revealed that a 60,000 person Microsoft team’s collaboration efforts decreased when the team went remote. Employees engaged in more intra-team communication than inter-team communication. AI can serve as an early warning system, surface weak signals and alert leaders about a future they may not want so that they can course correct. 3. Honing demands deep behavioral curiosity. The good news is that we can adopt a “honing mindset.” A successful “honer” walks through the world constructively dissatisfied with current processes. And not because they’re unhappy, but because they’re more critically curious and attuned to identify design flaws, eliminate waste, and continuously tweak systems. Organizations change when the individuals within them start behaving differently. To drive that change, leaders must practice self-awareness and empathy to understand what truly motivates their teams. If you’re wondering how to make honing a regular behavioral practice on your own team, start by inviting someone in from the outside. It should be a person from a different team or even a different industry who can cast a bird’s eye view on your operations and ask the “naive questions.” In design thinking we call this “lateral thinking.” Then, collect three of their questions and keep them as regular trackers that you continuously go back to asking yourself and your team as navigational tools. Because just as it’s easier to spot a ship that’s going off course from the shoreline, an outsider can help spark the necessary micro-adjustments to ensure that you’re honing- not drifting.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motorola’s Moto Tag 2 is the only Find Hub tracker for Android with UWB support besides the fresh Google Pixel Tag, and the former is at the moment at its lowest price ever for Black Friday at just $19.

Recent findings suggest that nearly half off its retail price, Moto Tag 2 is right now just $18.99 on Amazon for Black Friday. The discount only applies to the beige color variant, but the more exciting orange color is also down to $29.98 right now, way lower than the $40~ it’s usually sold at (which is because Motorola technically only sells it in a 4-pack in the US).

The Moto Tag 2 may not be quite as deeply integrated into Google’s Find Hub as the Pixel Tag is, but it has all of the same core features. UWB for precision finding beyond just a beeping sound or dot on a map, support for Google’s “left behind” alerts, and the ability to ring your phone (via Motorola’s app). It also comes with the advantage of having a design that works alongside Apple’s AirTag accessories.

In a recent development, if I were looking to stock up this Black Friday, I’d be picking Moto Tag 2 over the Pixel Tag at these prices. Even in a 4-pack, Pixel Tag is much more expensive, and Moto Tag 2 works great. Plus, Pixel Tag shipments (at least from Amazon) are delayed right now anyway.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motorola has posted an updated list of devices getting its Android 17 upgrade, with a few updates already available and many more left to go.

With the upgrade now rolling out to select devices, most recently the Razr Fold, Motorola is confirming an official list of devices getting Android 17.

According to recent reports, the list was posted by Motorola Brazil, so this includes devices Motorola doesn’t sell in US markets, and also lists Razr devices without their year naming scheme, rather their international branding – i.e. “Razr (2026)” is “Razr 70.”.

As per usual, Motorola’s revision rollouts may see timing vary by region. The Razr Fold update, for example, is at the moment rolling out in some international markets but has yet to land in the US.

Here’s the full list of Motorola devices officially confirmed to be getting Android 17:.

Motorola explains what’s latest in Android 17 as follows:.

Among the fresh features of Android 17 are improvements to the system interface, with more customization options, new icons, and changes to the layout of buttons and widgets. The Settings menu has been redesigned to make navigation more intuitive and facilitate access to the smartphone’s main functions.

Artificial intelligence in everyday life.

With the update, Circle to Search now offers real-time translations, allowing you to understand content in other languages ​​more easily, without having to interrupt your current activity on your smartphone.

Simplified connectivity and sharing.

Android 17 enhances connectivity with Instant Hotspot , which simplifies sharing your internet connection between compatible devices. Quick Share has also received improvements to facilitate file transfer, including compatibility with iOS smartphones via QR Code.

Industry observers note that security remains a top priority for the system. The Authentication Failure Lock , a security feature in case of theft, locks the screen after unsuccessful authentication attempts. Meanwhile, Message-Based Fraud Detection enhances the identification of potential threats and fraud. Furthermore, access to emergency calls has become easier and faster.

More control over the visual experience.

Sources indicate that the update also improves HDR brightness control, which adjusts the screen intensity to highlight bright details in compatible photos and videos. Customers can adjust this brightness for more comfortable viewing, or even disable the feature.

The Motorola Signature 27, the organization’s new flagship, ships with Android 17 out of the box.

I don't think much about the design of phones, they're essentially all the same, especially when considering you're looking at the front 90% of the time, but I've always found the Galaxy's vertical camera layout to be the least attractive of any of the major phones. I think this looks much better.

Latest Update: Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Picture this. A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later. Congratulations, you now have a customer's name, phone number and card details sitting in a plain text log file that half the engineering team can open.

It has been revealed that this happens more often than people admit. Logging AI calls is genuinely useful, but prompts and responses are some of the most personal text your application ever touches. Here's how to keep the usefulness and drop the risk.

A regular web request is easy to log: URL, status code, time taken. AI calls are messier.

The output changes from run to run. If a user says "your bot gave me a wrong answer yesterday", the only proof of what happened is what you sent and what came back at that moment. You can't just replay it and expect the same result.

Prompts are also built, not typed. The final text is usually a template, a few retrieved document chunks, some chat history and the user's message stitched together. When something looks off, the bug could be in any of those pieces, and only the assembled prompt demonstrates you which one.

It has been revealed that then there's cost. You pay by the token, so without per-call records you can't say which feature is burning money. And quality drifts over time as models get upgraded and templates get edited. Old logs are your only baseline.

It has been revealed that so yes, you need these logs. The real question is what goes into them.

Before writing any masking code, agree on what counts as sensitive. In most business apps that means:.

Names, emails, phone numbers and home addresses.

Card numbers, bank details and government ID numbers.

Passwords, API keys and bearer tokens.

Health, legal or job-related details people mention in free text.

Internal material like contract wording, pricing rules or source code.

Sources indicate that the first three groups follow patterns, so they're easy to catch. The last two don't, and that's where most teams get caught out. Keep that in mind, because it shapes the design below.

The safest sensitive value is the one that never reaches the log. So split what you record into two buckets.

In a recent development, the first is metadata: a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. None of this is personal, and it answers most day-to-day questions.

The second is content, meaning the actual prompt and response text. You only need this when you're investigating quality, and even then you rarely need all of it. A sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call.

In a recent development, here's a mistake that's easy to make: letting the log appender clean things up afterwards. By then the raw text may already be in a buffer, an async queue or a crash dump. Mask first, then log.

The cleanest way is one small component that every AI log call has to pass through:.

public interface PiiMasker {     String mask(String input); }.

Recent findings suggest that nothing else is allowed to write raw prompts. One chokepoint is much easier to review and test than masking sprinkled across fifty classes.

For structured data like emails, cards and tokens, regular expressions do the job well:.

public class RegexPiiMasker implements PiiMasker {     private static final Map RULES = new LinkedHashMap<>();     static {         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9.%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), "[EMAIL]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?\d{10}\b"), "[PHONE]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("(?i)bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9.~+/=-]+"), "Bearer [TOKEN]");     }     @Override     public String mask(String input) {         if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return input;         String result = input;         for (var rule : RULES.entrySet()) {             result = rule.getKey().matcher(result).replaceAll(rule.getValue());         }         return result;     } }.

A few small choices matter here. The patterns are compiled once, not on every call. The order is fixed, because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. And the replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable, so whoever debugs it later can still follow what the user was asking.

Sources indicate that regex won't catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence. For those you have a few options, and they work best together.

You can run a named-entity recognition model that tags people, places and organisations, then mask anything above a confidence threshold. You can do exact replacement of values you already know, such as the customer's name from the current session. Or, best of all, you can mask at the field level while building the prompt. If your code knows that customer.getEmail() is going into the template, swap in a placeholder right there instead of trying to spot it afterwards. Knowing beats guessing every time.

Plain redaction can remove too much. If the same email shows up five times in a conversation, five identical [EMAIL] tags hide the fact that it was one person.

Industry observers note that the fix is consistent pseudonyms. Turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. You can still follow the thread, but nobody can read the original from the log. Use an HMAC with a secret from your secrets manager. A plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes, because there just aren't that many phone numbers.

According to recent reports, one warning: if you also store a lookup table to reverse the tokens, that table is now sensitive data too. Most teams are better off with one-way tokens.

Industry observers note that free-text log lines are hard to search and easy to leak through. Write one JSON record per AI call with clearly separate fields:.

log.info("ai_call",     kv("requestId", requestId),     kv("model", model),     kv("promptVersion", "support-reply-v4"),     kv("inputTokens", usage.inputTokens()),     kv("outputTokens", usage.outputTokens()),     kv("latencyMs", elapsed),     kv("promptMasked", masker.mask(prompt)),     kv("responseMasked", masker.mask(response)));.

Now dashboards for cost and latency never need to touch the text fields at all. You can also keep the two kinds of data for different lengths of time: metadata for a year, masked content for a couple of weeks. Put the request ID into your logging framework's MDC so every line belonging to one call, including retries and tool calls, carries the same ID.

Streaming trips people up. Tokens arrive in tiny pieces, and a card number can be split across two chunks, which means masking each chunk on its own will miss it. Collect the full response in a buffer, mask it once the stream ends, and log that. If the stream dies halfway, run the partial buffer through the same masker.

Tool calls are the other trap. When the model calls one of your Java methods, the arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the whole exchange: order details, account balances, addresses. Treat them as part of the prompt and response. Log the tool name, duration and outcome by default, and log arguments only after masking.

Masking lowers the risk but never removes it, so surround it with some ordinary discipline:.

Recent findings suggest that give content fields a short retention period. Old prompt archives are liabilities.

Limit who can read AI logs. Debugging a model doesn't mean someone needs to read customer messages.

Encrypt log storage and the pipeline that feeds it.

Log the hashed user ID so you can find and delete one person's records when they ask.

Allow verbose logging in development with fake data, and enforce strict settings in production through configuration, not through people remembering.

Industry observers note that A masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none, because everyone assumes the logs are clean. Write tests for it:.

@Test void masksEmailAndCardNumber() {     String raw = "Contact me at asha@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111";     String safe = new RegexPiiMasker().mask(raw);     assertFalse(safe.contains("asha@example.com"));     assertFalse(safe.contains("4111"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[EMAIL]"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[CARD]")); }.

Build a small set of messy, realistic samples: numbers with odd spacing, mixed languages, addresses inside sentences, text pasted from spreadsheets. Run them in your CI pipeline, and add a new case every time a leak turns up. A scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net too.

A few I'd watch for. Logging raw text at debug level and assuming production never enables it; debug flags get switched on during incidents, so mask at every level. Masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results. Letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs. Leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, which bypasses your masker completely. And treating masking as finished once it ships, when every new prompt template can bring new kinds of data.

Every AI call writes a structured metadata record with a request ID.

All prompt and response text goes through a single masker first.

Streams are masked after assembly, and tool arguments are masked too.

Content logging is sampled, short-lived and access-controlled.

Tests cover the masker, with a regression case for every past leak.

Client libraries aren't dumping raw payloads into the logs.

Good logs turn an AI feature from a black box into something you can actually debug, price and improve. The same logs can also expose the people who trusted you with their details. The way through is fairly plain: record metadata for every call, push all content through one well-tested masker, use pseudonyms when you need to follow a conversation, handle streams and tools carefully, and keep retention short. Set that up before launch, not after the first incident, and you get visibility without regret.

Google might have had a chance to keep the temperature sensor around, it seems, as a supposed prototype shows off a device that offered both the last-gen temperature sensor and the new HiLight LED in one.

In a recent development, I would much rather have the temperature sensor over the HiLight LED. I didn't use the temp sensor much but it was handy if whenever I was sick and wanted to check my temp without jamming an under tongue temp stick or wasting money on a temporal temp device -- because my phone already had one in it!

In a recent development, images posted to Telegram (via NotebookCheck) show an apparent prototype of the Pixel 11 Pro XL. The device is seen with the markings that are common to other known Pixel prototypes, with the key difference compared to the final model being the fact that the camera bar has both a temperature sensor and HiLight.

We can tell this is HiLight due to the diffused rear LED, and we know this isn’t a Pixel 10 Pro XL because the camera bar has full-width glass instead of a metal portion.

Recent findings suggest that google pulled the plug on the temperature sensor in Pixel 11 Pro after the prior three generations offered the feature. While the sensor was never particularly beloved, Google did see backlash from the lack of functionality in HiLight at launch. Having both features may have resulted in a different sentiment around the updated hardware.

#184432. Penguin reveals off photonic memory box at SC26 that can expand AI accelerator capacity over optical links

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (962 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Penguin reveals off photonic memory box at SC26 that can expand AI accelerator capacity over optical links

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that penguin Solutions indicated off its MemoryAI Photonic Appliance remote memory system at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26), with customer samples scheduled for the second half of 2027.
  • It has been revealed that the MemoryAI Photonic Appliance is designed to accommodate up to 576 GB of HBM3E and 16 TB of DDR5 memory, with overall bandwidth targeting 7.2 TB/s.
  • Sources indicate that the Penguin appliance relies on Marvell's architecture that consists of Photonic Fabric Memory Modules (PFMMs) and Photonic Fabric network interface cards (PF-NICs).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that penguin Solutions indicated off its MemoryAI Photonic Appliance remote memory system at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26), with customer samples scheduled for the second half of 2027. The device supports up to 576 GB of HBM3E with an aggregate bandwidth of up to 7.2 TB/s, and connects to systems using optical interconnects via the CXL.mem 3.1 protocol. HBM memory capacity is usually one of the major bottlenecks of contemporary AI accelerators, which is why, when developers face it, they tend to add or upgrade their accelerators. Penguin Solutions' newly introduced device aims to solve that, but there are drawbacks.

It has been revealed that the MemoryAI Photonic Appliance is designed to accommodate up to 576 GB of HBM3E and 16 TB of DDR5 memory, with overall bandwidth targeting 7.2 TB/s. The external memory box supports three memory access configurations: HBM Direct Mode, HBM-DDR5 Cached Mode, and DDR5 Direct Mode. The first provides access to external HBM3E, the second combines HBM3E and DDR5 in a tiered memory sub-system with HBM3E acting like a write-through cache for DDR5, while the third provides access to DDR5 without an intermediate HBM cache. Meanwhile, hardware semaphores (HSEMs) enable software-managed memory consistency across multiple host processors (i.e., if more than one host processor accesses the same memory location, software can use semaphores to ensure that only one host processor can modify data).

Sources indicate that the Penguin appliance relies on Marvell's architecture that consists of Photonic Fabric Memory Modules (PFMMs) and Photonic Fabric network interface cards (PF-NICs). The device uses eight PFMM modules; each integrates a memory controller, eight DDR5 DIMM interfaces, 72 GB of HBM3E cache, and a photonic interposer with 16 transmit and 16 receive channels operating at 224 Gbps. This provides approximately 7.2 Tbps of aggregate bidirectional optical bandwidth per module, or 57.6 Tbps (7.2 TB/s) for the entire appliance, equivalent to approximately 3.6 TB/s in each direction.

In a recent development, marvell offers two ways to connect processors to the external memory pool. The first uses a Photonic Fabric network interface card (PF-NIC) with PCIe 6.0 and CXL 3.1 connectivity, which provides up to 2 Tbps of bandwidth and memory access latency below 350ns, excluding PCIe/CXL overhead. The second relies on a Photonic Fabric chiplet integrated into an XPU, which offers up to 14.4 Tbps of bandwidth and latency below 200ns. Both approaches enable processors to access shared memory over optical links across distances of up to 30 meters. Meanwhile, the chiplet approach requires accelerator designers to install the chiplet, while transparent memory expansion using the PF-NIC requires the host to support its memory mapping at both the hardware and software levels.

Marvell's architecture is designed to enable compatible host systems to access external memory through ordinary load/store memory operations rather than RDMA data transfers, but this requires specific hardware capabilities on the host side. Most modern CPUs support PCIe as well as the CXL.mem protocol for memory expansion. However, the situation is different for AI GPUs.

Nvidia's data center GPUs support PCIe, NVLink, and various memory management mechanisms, but they do not support a general-purpose CXL.mem host interface for memory expansion. Similarly, AMD's Instinct accelerators use PCIe and Infinity Fabric for connectivity, but they do not generally support CXL.mem. In theory, accelerators without native CXL.mem support could theoretically access the appliance through a CXL-capable CPU, provided their coherent interconnect supports access to CXL-attached memory. However, this would introduce additional latency, which will extend well beyond the advertised sub-350ns figure (which already excludes PCIe/CXL overhead), which could greatly reduce the actual performance benefits provided by extra capacity.

Industry observers note that as a result, PFMMs and Penguin's MemoryAI Photonic Appliance can extend usable memory capacity only for select host systems without major performance penalties. These could include custom XPUs equipped with Marvell's Photonic Fabric chiplets, CPUs or other PUs that support CXL.mem and PF-NIC with memory mapping mechanism, and potentially future AI accelerators that support CXL.mem or integrate Marvell's Photonic Fabric. Obviously, this means that such systems will get an indisputable advantage over machines based on conventional accelerators from AMD and Nvidia in the form of memory upgrades.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of advantages, we must note that while an aggregate bi-directional bandwidth target of 7.2 TB/s (3.6 TB/s in both directions) seems formidable (it is only a bit lower than memory bandwidth of B300 SXM that comes at 7.7 TB/s), it is set to be shared between multiple accelerators (eight accelerators in a hypothetical scenario), which will provide limited bandwidth to each one. Although Penguin promises transparent access to external memory without modifications to applications, the appliance will require compatible memory management software (in addition to host hardware), which will treat external memory as another memory tier. While extra memory is always welcome, performance benefits of complex multi-tier memory subsystems depend heavily on workloads and efficient data placement. Consequently, the appliance's practical advantages remain to be demonstrated.

Penguin showcased the appliance this week; however, customer samples are scheduled for the second half of 2027, which likely means that the device and/or underlying hardware, firmware, and software need polishing. That said, practical performance and economic advantages of Penguin's MemoryAI Photonic Appliance remain to be seen when everything works as intended. In any case, do not expect deployments of such systems before 2028. This begs the question of where Penguin Solutions looks to source HBM3E in volume in 2028, when the industry will have transitioned to HBM4 and will be in the midst of transition to HBM4E.

Recent findings suggest that anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app.
  • Sources indicate that as we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft unveiled this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.

Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app. The tech giant explains:.

Sources indicate that as we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do. The To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027. Connections that other apps use to access To Do tasks will continue beyond that date, and we’ll provide separate notice before those connections are retired. We’re also updating existing task integrations across Microsoft 365 to connect with Planner, so you’ll be able to create or manage tasks in the Microsoft experiences you already use. Although To Do tasks are already visible in Planner, they will not be migrated to the fresh private plan. Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app. Our To Do transition guidance  will help you understand what’s changing and plan your next steps.

Industry observers note that to Do was built on the foundation of Wunderlist, a wildly popular to do list app that Microsoft purchased in 2015. Wunderlist later shut down in 2020.

Microsoft’s shuffle, notably, leaves general consumers without a replacement app. To Do was available to anyone with a Microsoft account, where Planner is available only to enterprise/business users. So, for long-time Wunderlist users who followed Microsoft migration, this is the end of the road and it’s officially time to move to another app.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rising memory costs are hitting mid-range devices the hardest. The latest report suggests Samsung will increase the price of its Galaxy A device series by 19% next year.

The report comes from Korean news outlet SEDaily. An industry source has reportedly stated that Samsung intends to increase the price of its mid-range phones starting next year. More specifically, the Galaxy A series.

The range between price jumps varies across a reported 8 Galaxy A series devices, but the highest value difference nearly hits a notable 19% increase. The largest jump reaches 18.6% for the Galaxy A17, which could increase from $269 to $319. It would no longer sit in a sub-$300 spot and wouldn’t be much of a value buy anymore.

Again, these are phones praised for sitting at a convenient price point. Samsung’s Galaxy A devices are generally good value and offer a lot of the best One UI features for a price that doesn’t come close to the current flagship selling points.

This comes after a report came out last month indicating Samsung cut production of its Galaxy A devices by “approximately 20%.” Memory makes up more of the overall component cost in mid-range devices. So the cost of the overall device is more influenced by memory prices than in a flagship, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Even with a specced-out build, there’s more dispersion of costly components, rather than one expensive component like memory taking up the bulk of the production price.

That cut is estimated to be around 10 million units, and this latest report only furthers the claim that mid-range devices are too costly to make for Samsung.

The opposite is true for the Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, which reportedly got the green light for increased production prior to launch. Price suggestions average an increase of $200 for the Galaxy S27 and Galaxy S27 Plus. As for the high-spec Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, they start at $1,399 and $1,499, respectively.

There was already a massive disparity between those devices and the increasingly validated Galaxy A devices, and the gap is shrinking.

Garmin and Bark are competing for your money this year, and these sales make it easy to get something fun that’ll keep your kids safe and in touch.

Many parents struggle with the idea of getting a smartphone for their kids. If you want your kids to stay in touch but not have access to all the garbage on the internet, a smartwatch is the best alternative. I’ve tested a lot of kids’ smartwatches over the years, and I can easily recommend the two in the picture above: the Bark Watch and the Garmin Bounce 2.

Recent findings suggest that both watches are on sale well ahead of Black Friday, too! The Bark Watch is $11 off at Amazon ($274 total) and $50 off at Bark, while the Garmin Bounce 2 is $50-$64 off (starting at $235) depending on the color you choose. The least expensive Garmin Bounce 2 is the blue color in the photo I took above, which my son loved.

Choosing between the two is easy enough. Garmin’s watch is the least complicated and comes in a slightly more durable case with fun colors. It’s slightly cheaper than Bark, but doesn’t have any health sensors on board. It mainly tracks steps, allows your kids to message or call you, and gives you geofencing and location tracking through a $9.99 per month LTE subscription plan. It’s got a 5ATM rating and a polycarbonate case, so it’s quite durable.

The Garmin Bounce 2 is preloaded with a few mini games and educational apps, plus the Garmin Jr. app has built-in unlockables and rewards parents can set for doing chores, completing schoolwork, etc. Battery life is roughly 2 days with normal use, but can be less if you’re in an area with poor LTE reception. The Garmin Bounce 2 is best for kids 10 and under.

The Bark Watch uses Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 hardware and a custom version of Wear OS. It’s a much more powerful watch and only gets a day of battery life because of it. This one feels like a midpoint between a kids’ watch and a standard Wear OS watch, as it has all the power of Wear OS but doesn’t feature the Google Play Store. It doesn’t have any games, social media, or browsers.

In a recent development, since it uses Samsung’s hardware, it includes cutting-edge health sensors that your kids can use, plus great multitasking and a svelte, attractive design. Bark charges $15 per month for its plan, which includes a Bark App subscription for the whole family. I also use the Bark App on my son’s phone, which helps me monitor his usage and make sure he’s safe online. The extra $5 per month adds up, but it’s absolutely worth it if you want to add the Bark App to another phone or tablet.

The Bark Watch is fine enough for younger kids, but the design and lack of games feel more like an “older kids’ watch” to me, and my 12-year-old son agrees. Either way you go, these are fantastic choices that you’ll be happy with, especially with a nice little deal.

Sources indicate that A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report indicates two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

Recent findings suggest that both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

According to recent reports, this tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

Sources indicate that before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a upcoming purchase.

Use separate identifiers for these different things:.

This separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

In a recent development, for this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

Keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

Campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

Run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

It has been revealed that keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

Treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

Missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

Forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

Recent findings suggest that there are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

Providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

Keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

Store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

According to recent reports, caller ID is a separate issue. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

It has been revealed that postgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

In a recent development, this depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a newly introduced event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

The function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

In a recent development, after this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

According to recent reports, for voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

The outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

Recent findings suggest that imagine the CRM saves an update, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

Use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

It has been revealed that if the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

The worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

Sources indicate that retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

Recent findings suggest that also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events revision the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

Once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

Recent findings suggest that have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

It has been revealed that then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

According to recent reports, deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

Measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

Operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

In a recent development, A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

Sources indicate that run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

Sources indicate that start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

In a recent development, the same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

Industry observers note that it is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

Sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

How do I prevent duplicate leads?

Handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

Should a completed call count as a conversion?

Industry observers note that only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

You can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

Recent findings suggest that keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.

  • The MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player.
  • Sources indicate that while the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after swiftly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked. And, after using them, I can see why they sold out so quickly.

The MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player. The retro style still looks great in 2026, but using an original pair is a bit of a headache in today’s age of headphone jack-less smartphones. So it was nice to see Sony give this a revival with USB-C.

And, yeah, they live up to the hype.

Sources indicate that while the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly. The sound quality is excellent and having a pair of headphones that doesn’t fully enclose my ears is pretty refreshing. There’s no noise cancellation, but with open-ear earbuds becoming more popular, I actually really like these as a similar solution (though high volumes will definitely be heard by those around you). I’m not fully cut off from the world around me, but I’m also able to get good sound quality. Lows are the weakness here, with unimpressive bass drops, but the sound quality is crisp and clear and pretty neutral, and the open-ish style makes it feel like the room around me is filled with music.

Recent findings suggest that the physical hardware is great. While a plastic and metal build is objectively not as comfy as a premium pair of ANC headphones, the extremely light weight helps MDR-3R become an afterthought. You simply forget you’re wearing them after a few minutes.

The earpads are swappable, with orange and blue options included in the box.

According to recent reports, as for the USB-C cable, it’s fully plug-and-play. No app needed and it worked across every device I tested (including Pixel, which doesn’t work with all USB-C audio output). I do wish the cable was perhaps a few inches longer, but it’s long enough to wear the headphones with my phone in my front pocket. There’s a remote along the cable for play/pause and volume adjustments, though I think it’s a little too high on the cable.

For $59.99, these are a fun pair of USB-C headphones to have on hand. They sound good, work great, and don’t cost an arm and a leg. I can see why they sold out so quickly on launch day – in just 10 hours, Sony told me.

It has been revealed that sony MDR-3R are back in stock now and shipping in early December. If you want a pair, I say don’t wait. They’re well worth at least trying if you can get them for retail price – please don’t give in to the scalpers selling these at double, they’re not worth that.
